The long way to the set

I came to film the long way. It was the right way.

Film wasn't where I started. I studied Food Science and Technology, managed a company's daily operations, and worked in a bank, where people brought me their complaints and expected me to fix them.

None of it looked like preparation for a film set. All of it was.

Management taught me that people lean on whoever keeps things running. The bank taught me to stay steady with someone who is frustrated, and to solve the problem in front of me. Food Science trained my eye for process: right order, careful detail.

Then I walked onto a set. A film set runs on exactly those things, with a camera attached.

A production does not stop being complicated just because the camera is ready.

Script supervision was where I began in film, guarding continuity. From there the work widened: first AD, production manager, line producer, director, producer. The same discipline now supports clients remotely, as a virtual assistant.

The long way round

Four chapters, one habit.

  1. 2001UKconceptResponsibility came early. As manager, I looked after operations, salaries and daily activity, and learned that people lean on whoever keeps things running.
  2. 2003 to 2004Intercontinental Bank PlcListening, for a living. Handling customer complaints taught me to stay steady with frustrated people and to solve the problem in front of me.
  3. 2017 to 2020Zuri24 MediaThe set. As script supervisor, I found work that needed everything I'd practised: attention, order, and a way with people.
  4. TodayMore seats at the tableFirst AD, production manager, line producer, director, producer, and virtual assistant for clients who need the same order off set.

How I work

Different seats, same set.

Script supervision

I catch what no one notices until it's wrong: a prop that moved, a line that changed, a performance that doesn't match the take before. Continuity is how a story keeps its promise.

First assistant directing

The seat between the schedule and the set. I help coordinate the day so everyone knows what's happening, what comes next, and what just changed.

Production management and line production

Time, resources, people, logistics. I plan, schedule and coordinate, and I try to meet problems before they meet the camera.

Virtual assistance

Same discipline, different location. Scheduling, communication, research, admin, follow-ups and task management, kept moving for clients who can't afford loose ends.

A Heart on the Line

Five days in, the first AD resigned.

I joined A Heart on the Line as script supervisor. My job was the story's continuity: what we had shot, what matched, what had to carry forward.

Then, five days into production, the first AD resigned.

A set does not pause for that. The schedule is still running. Cast and crew are still waiting. Someone has to know what happens next, and say it steadily.

I stepped into the first AD role and helped lead the production day. There was no quiet week to prepare. What I had was everything the other seats had taught me: the script, the schedule and the people.

The lesson stayed with me: be ready for the seat you didn't plan to take.

Role
Script Supervisor, then First Assistant Director
What it shows
Composure, production knowledge and the ability to lead when the plan changes.

The Party

A mystery only works if the details agree.

In The Party, everyone is a suspect, and everyone tells the night differently. The film moves through many points of view, with storylines wound around each other.

That changes what continuity means. It stops being "what was in her hand in the last scene" and becomes "which version of the night is this, and how does it connect to the others?" The audience should chase the puzzle. They should never catch the mistakes. That was my work as script supervisor.

Role
Script Supervisor

Renee

When a shoot turns difficult, this is how I behave.

Renee was a hard production. Circumstances were difficult, and not everyone around it was pulling the same way. Some people tried to undermine the work.

As line producer, I couldn't afford to react. I had to read the situation, decide carefully, and keep people and resources organised enough for the work to continue. The project is still a work in progress.

Role
Line Producer
What it asked for
Judgment, leadership, problem solving and resourcefulness.
